oneliners.1.1.33: Red Winemaking: a family of 10 wine entries, including Destemming, Whole-cluster fermentation and Cold soak.
oneliners.1.1.33.1: Separating grape berries from their stems before crushing or fermentation.
oneliners.1.1.33.2: Fermenting red grapes with their stems still attached.
oneliners.1.1.33.3: Holding crushed red grapes cold before fermentation to extract color and aroma.
oneliners.1.1.33.4: Whole, uncrushed grapes ferment inside a CO2-filled vessel, giving fruity, low-tannin reds (as in Beaujolais).
oneliners.1.1.33.5: Pumping fermenting red wine from the bottom of the tank over the skin cap to extract color and tannin.
oneliners.1.1.33.6: Pushing the floating skin cap down into fermenting red wine to extract color and tannin.
oneliners.1.1.33.7: Draining fermenting red juice off the skins into another tank, then pouring it back over the cap to extract gently.
oneliners.1.1.33.8: Leaving red wine on its skins after fermentation ends to change tannin texture.
oneliners.1.1.33.9: Bleeding off juice from a red-wine tank early to make rosé and concentrate the remaining red.
oneliners.1.1.33.10: Bacterial conversion of malic acid into lactic acid, softening a wine's acidity.
oneliners.1.1.34: White & Rosé Winemaking: a family of 8 wine entries, including Whole-bunch pressing, Skin contact and Cold settling.
oneliners.1.1.34.1: Pressing whole clusters without crushing, giving cleaner, lower-phenolic juice.
oneliners.1.1.34.2: Leaving juice in contact with grape skins; for white grapes this makes 'orange' or amber wine.
oneliners.1.1.34.3: Letting freshly pressed white juice rest cold so solids settle out before fermentation.
oneliners.1.1.34.4: Fermenting at low temperatures (often around 10–16 °C for whites) to keep fresh, fruity aromas.
oneliners.1.1.34.5: Leaving wine in contact with its spent yeast after fermentation to build texture and flavor.
oneliners.1.1.34.6: Stirring the lees (spent yeast) back into a wine during aging to add texture.
oneliners.1.1.34.7: Rosé made by pressing red grapes right away, giving brief skin contact and pale color.
oneliners.1.1.34.8: Preventing malolactic fermentation (for example by cold, sulfur dioxide or filtration) so the wine keeps its sharper malic acidity.
oneliners.1.1.35: Sparkling Methods: a family of 8 wine entries, including Traditional method, Tank method and Ancestral method.
oneliners.1.1.35.1: Sparkling method in which the second fermentation happens in the bottle sold (as in Champagne and Cava).
oneliners.1.1.35.2: Sparkling method with the second fermentation in a pressurized tank (common for Prosecco).
oneliners.1.1.35.3: Sparkling method where wine is bottled before primary fermentation finishes, trapping its CO2.
oneliners.1.1.35.4: Sparkling method with second fermentation in bottle, after which the wine is transferred to a tank, filtered and rebottled.
oneliners.1.1.35.5: Gradually turning and tilting sparkling-wine bottles so sediment collects in the neck before disgorgement.
oneliners.1.1.35.6: Removing the frozen plug of yeast sediment from a traditional-method sparkling wine bottle.
oneliners.1.1.35.7: Sugar-and-wine mixture added after disgorgement, setting a sparkling wine's sweetness level.
oneliners.1.1.35.8: Presence of dissolved CO2, which makes wine sparkling.
oneliners.1.1.36: Fortified & Oxidative: a family of 5 wine entries, including Mutage, Post-fermentation fortification and Flor.

oneliners.1.1.36.2: Adding spirit after fermentation has finished, leaving a dry base that may be sweetened later.
oneliners.1.1.36.3: A layer of yeast on the surface of Fino and Manzanilla Sherry that protects the wine from oxidation.
oneliners.1.1.36.4: Aging with deliberate oxygen contact, giving nutty, dried-fruit flavors (such as Oloroso, tawny Port).
oneliners.1.1.36.5: Madeira method of heating wine in tanks (estufas) to speed up aging.
oneliners.1.1.37: Finishing: a family of 4 wine entries, including Fining, Filtration and Cold stabilization.

oneliners.1.1.37.4: Combining wines from different grapes, vineyards, vessels or vintages to build balance and a consistent style.

oneliners.1.1.41: Toast Levels: a family of 7 wine entries, including Light toast, Medium toast and Medium-plus toast.
